prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which brought optical atomic time-keeping to the 10^-18 level of accuracy

statement.case_for: I keep B015 as a single-part prize. The lattice clock is a distinct, nameable architecture: neutral atoms held at a magic wavelength, where the light shift cancels on the clock transition, so that the statistics of many atoms are combined with Lamb-Dicke confinement. That is not a refinement of a trapped single ion, where the signal comes from one particle and the limit is statistical, and it is not the frequency comb, which is a ruler for optical frequencies and not a reference. The round-1 exchange has strengthened rather than weakened my view on three points. First, nobody disputes the science or the maturity: all eight files call it reproduced near 1e-18 and the chair records the credit as the least contested on the shortlist. Second, the independence of the 1e-18 claim does not rest on my say-so; it rests on comparisons between laboratories and between species, which is the kind of evidence a committee can ask for in the nomination record. Third, the two-name credit maps onto two separable contributions, Katori for the magic-wavelength concept and the first strontium lattice clock, Ye for taking the systematic uncertainty to the performance frontier. A citation worded around the lattice concept and the accuracy achieved, and not around combs or clocks in general, answers the novelty question put by the chair. I do not argue that an instrument advance should automatically outrank a discovery of nature; I argue that here the instrument advance is a new physical scheme with a clean credit and confirmed performance.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against is still the overlap with the 2005 (Hall, Hansch) and 2012 (Wineland, Haroche) prizes, and a member who weighs it heavily can reasonably place a field not yet honoured ahead of this one. I accept that the answer I give, a distinct magic-wavelength architecture, is a judgement about what counts as a separate invention, and that Danielsson's distinction between a measurement capability and a new phenomenon is a real difference of scientific taste and not an error. Second, two names leave out groups with real claims (Lemonde at SYRTE, Lisdat at PTB, Ludlow, Lemke and others in Ye's group, and the single-ion clocks), and I have no third name that I can defend without displacing one of the two. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened; I regard it as an application milestone decided by another body, but it is a legitimate timing argument for those who want to wait. Fourth, my own declared link to the Boulder laboratory means my support should be read with that in mind, and the other five supporters give independent reasons.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B015 sixth because of overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and moved to B018 as the strongest condensed-matter case, with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan as the credit; he also says he cannot verify the Katori and Ye attribution from the supplied material.
responses.response: The chair put your overlap question as the test, so I will answer it directly. The 2005 prize recognised the comb and precision laser spectroscopy, and the 2012 prize recognised the control of single ions. The lattice clock is neither: its defining idea is that a lattice at the magic wavelength lets millions of neutral atoms be interrogated with no first-order light shift and no recoil or Doppler broadening, which a single ion cannot offer and a free atomic ensemble cannot achieve. A citation that says exactly that, and does not mention combs or clocks in general, separates it from both. On B018, I agree that the discovery is real and that it is the most influential condensed-matter concept in the pool. My objection is still credit: Mele co-authored the Z2 papers, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction, and you yourself note that Fu, Kane and Mele for the three-dimensional case are also outside three names. I also note your 2016-prize caveat. Where the committee can only name three, a defensible clean credit counts for more than I would like it to, and on that criterion B015 is stronger. I do not claim B018 is the weaker science.

responses.point: Pearce supports B015 for attribution and independent confirmation, says 'overdue' should not be a ranking argument, and asks that my Hall-laboratory connection be recorded formally and my support weighted accordingly.
responses.response: I accept both points. 'Overdue' was a poor word in my opening and I withdraw it as an argument; urgency is not merit, and the case I rely on is the mechanism, the credit and the confirmation. On the connection, I agree it should be recorded formally and I have restated it in my conflict note below. I would add that the committee does not need my testimony on the confirmation: it can ask for the inter-laboratory comparison record across species and institutions, which is independent of any one laboratory, and your own, Lindroth's and Mehlig's files rely on that same argument. If members consider that my link should reduce the weight given to my vote, I would not object, because B015 has five other supporters whose reasoning does not depend on mine. I also take your honest point that B014 is stronger on opening a new observational window; I judge it weaker on credit, not on significance.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps B014 first as a discovery of nature, concedes that B015 is cleaner on attribution and maturity, and asks whether the lattice idea is a separate achievement or an extension of work already recognised.
responses.response: I can only say what I would put in a citation. The magic-wavelength lattice makes the clock transition insensitive to the trapping light while the atoms are confined to the Lamb-Dicke regime, and this lets many atoms be averaged at once, which is the reason the systematic uncertainty has fallen to 1e-18. That is a new route to a measurement and also, through comparisons of clocks at different heights and between species, a probe of relativistic redshift and of possible variation of constants, so it is not only an instrument improvement. On B014 you give the fairest statement of the choice: if the committee puts breadth of discovery ahead of clean attribution, B014 is the right prize. My concern is that Halzen and Karle stand for a collaboration of hundreds with the AMANDA and DUMAND precursors, and the source evidence you would like in the citation is still statistically modest, so I would limit any B014 citation to the diffuse flux. I list B014 as my first alternative for that reason, and I would not call the committee wrong to choose it.

responses.point: Mehlig supports B015, warns that the broad consensus may reflect familiarity and not an independent judgement of discovery value, and asks whether the credit leaves out co-developers such as Ludlow and Lemke.
responses.response: Your familiarity worry is fair, and the answer is that the evidence should be independent of the committee's taste: the 1e-18 uncertainty has been reproduced in more than one laboratory and species, and clock comparisons make the check external. On the credit, I looked for a better two- or three-name set and could not find one that I can defend. Ludlow and Lemke worked in Ye's group, which fits Ye's role as the leader who took performance to the frontier, and adding Lemonde or Lisdat would force us to drop Katori or Ye, who have the two clearest separable roles. I therefore think two names are a simplification, as every prize credit is, and not an injustice. I note your caution on B032, and I agree that giving B015 does not preempt an ultracold-atom prize later.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate invention from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion work, which is a judgement and not a measurement.

Whether two names are an acceptable simplification given the contributions of SYRTE, PTB, NIST, Ludlow, Lemke and the single-ion clock groups; I cannot name a third person within the limit who does not displace Katori or Ye.
Whether the committee prefers breadth of discovery (B014) to clean attribution, a difference of judgement that I do not claim to resolve, and which would change my first alternative into the prize.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should count as confirmation of maturity or as a reason to wait; I see it as an application milestone decided by another body.
My recollection of the lattice-clock history and the latest uncertainty values comes from general knowledge and is not verified against the nomination material here.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure, as Pearce and the chair's summary asked to be recorded: during my doctoral period I made a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye (credited in B015) is associated with that laboratory. I regard this as professional background and not a personal relationship with Ye, and I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye; I have no objection to its being recorded formally, and to the committee weighing my support accordingly. I also hold a WACQT programme-management role and have European quantum-memory and quantum-optics contacts, which touch B039, B009 and B032 as a field (relevant to my alternative B009) but not any credited individual. I have documented colleagues at Lund (Rippe, Walther, Kinos) who are not candidates. No other specific conflict is apparent.
